# Figures — captions and provenance

**Generated by `python -m src.plots` (Phase 9). Do not edit by hand — it is rewritten on
every run.** Each entry carries the report-ready caption and the exact rows of
`reports/metrics.csv` every mark was drawn from — or, for the confusion matrices, checked
against — keyed on `(run_id, model, regime)`.

Source log: `reports/metrics.csv` (MD5 `116def31c6bca1bb788d4a86f9cc976e`) — every scalar. The 2x2
confusion counts, which that file's frozen 14-column header has no room for, come from
`reports/confusion_matrices.json` (MD5 `e6525580adbf1854cf30ce729e82f644`), written by
`evaluate.run_phase6()`. This module reads both and writes neither; where they overlap they
are cross-checked against each other before anything is drawn.

**Δ sign convention throughout: `Δ = in_distribution − cross_era`, i.e. what the model
*lost* — positive means degraded.** This is `evaluate.metric_deltas()` and what `./run.sh`
prints.

## Figure 1 — `drift_indist_vs_crossera.png`

**Figure 1. Cross-era collapse of a 2015-trained intrusion detector (RQ1).** Each model is trained once on the UNSW-NB15 (2015) training fold and evaluated unchanged in two regimes: in-distribution on the UNSW-NB15 test set (n=82,332; 44.94% normal / 55.06% attack) and zero-shot cross-era on TON_IoT (2019–20; n=211,043; 23.69% normal / 76.31% attack), with no refitting of either the model or the preprocessor. Panel (a) leads because ROC-AUC is insensitive to the change in class balance: every real model falls from 0.8811–0.9788 in-distribution to 0.1846–0.3534 cross-era, i.e. *below* the 0.5000 chance line, so the learned score ranking does not merely stop working but runs backwards (a rank inversion, not a decay); the largest loss is Δ +0.7775. Panel (b) must be read against the two dashed majority-class lines: a dummy that predicts "attack" everywhere scores F1 0.7102 on UNSW-test and 0.8656 on TON_IoT purely because the attack share rises from 55.06% to 76.31%, so part of every F1 movement is prevalence rather than drift. Δ = in-distribution − cross-era throughout, i.e. what the model *lost*: positive means degraded. The two ablation conditions (`phase6-crossera-no_proto`, `phase6-crossera-no_conn_state`) are excluded from this figure by construction.

## Figure 2 — `recovery_curve.png`

**Figure 2. How little modern data undoes the cross-era collapse (RQ2).** TON_IoT is split once (seed 42, stratified) into a permanent 105,521-row test half and a disjoint 105,522-row fine-tune pool; every point on both panels is scored on that same frozen half, so the labelling budget is the only variable along x. The zero-budget point is re-measured on the frozen half rather than carried over from the cross-era run of Figure 1, which was scored on all 211,043 TON_IoT rows and therefore included the pool. A budget of 1% (1,055 labelled flows) lifts every model from ROC-AUC 0.1847–0.3519 to 0.8845–0.9979, clearing the majority-class floor of 0.5000 in every case, and the 25% budget closes 99.5%–100.0% of the remaining ROC-AUC gap to each model's own ceiling. The F1 panel is the one that needs its floor: a dummy predicting "attack" everywhere already scores F1 0.8656 on this half, so only recovery well above that line means anything. Ceilings are each model's own adaptation mechanism at the full pool and are shown past the axis break; the MLP's is set by its mechanism rather than by data — freezing both hidden layers costs 0.0172 ROC-AUC against the same architecture retrained end to end, logged separately as `phase7-recovery-ceiling-no_freeze` and excluded from this figure. A few points sit marginally above their own ceiling at the larger budgets (by at most 0.0007, i.e. run-to-run noise).

## Figure 3 — `confusion_matrices.png`

**Figure 3. Where the cross-era predictions go (RQ1).** Confusion matrices for all six models in both regimes of Figure 1, from the same single fit per model: in-distribution on the UNSW-NB15 test set (n=82,332; 55.06% attack) and zero-shot cross-era on TON_IoT (n=211,043; 76.31% attack). Cell order is [[tn, fp], [fn, tp]] (sklearn `labels=[0, 1]`, 1 = attack); rows are the true class and columns the predicted class, and each cell is annotated with its count and with that count as a share of its own true-class row, because the two regimes are measured on sets of different size and balance and raw counts do not compare across them. Reading down a column shows the RQ1 result as predictions rather than scores: the shaded mass leaves the diagonal. Attack recall falls from 82.4%–94.8% to 15.1%–42.4%, and the balanced accuracy printed above each matrix — the mean of the two diagonal shares, and a logged column — drops from 0.7400–0.8972 to 0.2178–0.3374, i.e. below 0.5000 for every real model: averaged over the two classes they predict the wrong label more often than the right one. The majority-class dummy is the control that shows this is not simply the change in prevalence — it predicts "attack" on all 211,043 cross-era rows, so its entire matrix sits in the right-hand column in both regimes and its balanced accuracy is exactly 0.5000 in each. Matrices are the ones `evaluate.run_phase6()` computed under `run_id=phase6-crossera` (the full d=22 feature set; both ablation conditions are excluded by construction), persisted to `reports/confusion_matrices.json`; every matrix was checked against the accuracy, precision, recall, balanced accuracy and prevalence of its own row of `reports/metrics.csv` before being drawn.
